chromosomal-and-genetic-disorders.name: Chromosomal and genetic disorders
chromosomal-and-genetic-disorders.scope: Down syndrome (trisomy 21), Turner syndrome (45,X0), Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY), Fragile X syndrome (FMR1 trinucleotide repeat), Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes, DiGeorge syndrome (22q11 deletion)
chromosomal-and-genetic-disorders.core: Recognize syndromic combinations of growth, cognition, gonadal function, dysmorphism, and congenital malformations; confirm with the correct genetic test.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Advanced maternal age: meiotic nondisjunction; balanced parental translocation: recurrent aneuploid pregnancy
Family expansion history: repeat disorders; microdeletions often de novo

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Down** (trisomy 21): hypotonia, upslanting fissures, epicanthal folds, macroglossia, single palmar crease, AV septal defect
DiGeorge: conotruncal defect, cleft palate, absent thymus, hypocalcemic tetany
Turner: newborn hand/foot lymphedema, redundant nuchal skin; later nevi
**Williams** (7q11.23 deletion): overfriendly, elfin facies, hyperacusis, intellectual disability, supravalvular stenosis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: ★ **Genomic imprinting**: parent-specific expression; deletion or uniparental disomy can disrupt the active copy
22q11 deletion disrupts pharyngeal pouch development → T-cell deficiency and hypoparathyroidism

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Suspected Down, Turner, Klinefelter → **karyotype**; prenatal screening alone never establishes diagnosis
Microarray: microdeletion; targeted repeat analysis: fragile X; methylation testing: imprinting disorders
Down: assess heart, hearing, vision, thyroid; DiGeorge: calcium and lymphocyte subsets

rows.label: Tx
items: Early developmental services, speech support; repair congenital defects
Turner: growth hormone then estrogen/progestin; Klinefelter: testosterone after endocrine assessment
Prader-Willi: supervised food access; Angelman: seizure management; DiGeorge: calcium and infection management

rows.label: Complications
items: Down: duodenal atresia (double bubble), leukemia, early Alzheimer disease, atlantoaxial instability
Turner: coarctation, bicuspid valve, aortic dissection; Klinefelter: infertility, breast cancer
Prader-Willi: severe obesity; DiGeorge: severe infections and later psychiatric disease

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Genetic counseling**: recurrence depends on nondisjunction, translocation, imprinting mechanism, or repeat expansion
Avoid live vaccines with severe T-cell deficiency; use irradiated blood for profound immunodeficiency

rows.label: Mimics
items: Noonan syndrome: Turner-like habitus, normal chromosomes; either sex, pulmonic stenosis
Congenital hypothyroidism: hypotonia and delayed development; abnormal newborn thyroid screen
Constitutional delay: delayed bone age; no edema or nevi
Rett: girls with regression; MECP2 variant

table.title: Distinctive genotype–phenotype pairs
rows: Short female, webbed neck, streak ovaries, primary amenorrhea
Tall male, small firm testes, gynecomastia, high FSH/LH
FMR1 CGG expansion at X fragile site; silencing
Long face, large ears, macroorchidism, autism-like behavior
IUGR, clenched overlapping fingers, prominent occiput, micrognathia, VSD

chromosomal-and-genetic-disorders.evidence: Not checked online; established genetics teaching.

delirium.name: Delirium
delirium.scope: Diagnostic criteria, precipitating causes (infection, metabolic, drugs), workup, management and prevention
delirium.core: Acute fluctuating inattention with altered cognition or awareness indicates delirium and requires a search for physiologic triggers.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Older age, baseline dementia, frailty, sensory impairment, hospitalization or recent surgery
Infection (UTI, pneumonia, wound), hypoxia, metabolic derangement, dehydration, retention, constipation and uncontrolled pain
Anticholinergics (amitriptyline), meperidine, other opioids, steroids, sedatives; alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal

rows.label: Clues
items: Disorganized thinking, sleep–wake reversal, hallucinations; hyperactive, hypoactive or mixed presentation
★ Hypoactive withdrawal/lethargy easily missed; **test attention**, not orientation alone
Digit span, months backward or inability to sustain conversation reveals attentional deficit
**Asterixis** → toxic-metabolic encephalopathy of any cause, not only hepatic failure

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Systemic stress and drug effects disrupt vulnerable brain networks and neurotransmitter balance
Multiple small precipitating factors can exceed low cognitive reserve

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CAM**: acute/fluctuating course + inattention + disorganized thinking or altered consciousness
Immediate glucose, oxygenation, vitals; focused neurologic examination, medication review and collateral baseline
CBC, electrolytes, renal/liver function; ECG, chest imaging guided by findings; wound/sepsis signs → **blood cultures**
CT head for focal deficit, trauma or unexplained reduced consciousness; LP for suspected CNS infection
Fever, urinary symptoms or dementia → **urinalysis** for UTI before CT/LP; bacteriuria alone doesn't prove cause

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Treat precipitant**; reorient, restore hearing/glasses, hydrate, mobilize and normalize sleep
Calm environment and familiar support; remove unnecessary catheters and avoid physical restraints
★ Severe distress or danger despite de-escalation → short course **haloperidol**, check QT/EPS risk
Parkinson disease/Lewy body dementia → avoid potent dopamine blockers; specialist-guided alternative
Benzodiazepines generally worsen delirium; reserve for withdrawal or selected seizures/catatonia

rows.label: Complications
items: Falls, aspiration, prolonged hospitalization, functional decline, persistent cognitive impairment and increased mortality
Antipsychotics may prolong QT; sedation may conceal clinical deterioration

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Multicomponent prevention: orientation, daytime activity, sleep protection, hydration, pain control and drug review
Minimize nighttime interruptions and unnecessary sedatives; encourage family engagement

rows.label: Mimics
items: Dementia: chronic progression; attention relatively preserved early
Depression: sustained mood symptoms without fluctuating consciousness
Primary psychosis: usually preserved attention and alertness

depressive-disorders.name: Depressive disorders
depressive-disorders.scope: Major depressive disorder criteria, depression in older adults, bereavement vs MDD, pharmacotherapy, psychotherapy, suicide risk
depressive-disorders.core: Persistent low mood or loss of pleasure with neurovegetative and cognitive symptoms, causing clinically significant distress or impaired function.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior episodes, family history, chronic illness/pain, substance use, postpartum period, social isolation
Older adults: disability, bereavement, polypharmacy; somatic presentations

rows.label: Clues
items: SIGECAPS: sleep, interest, guilt, energy, concentration, appetite, psychomotor change, suicidality
Psychotic depression: delusions/hallucinations only during mood episodes, often guilt or nihilism
★ **Suicide risk**: prior attempt, intent, plan, means, agitation, psychosis, intoxication
Youth: **irritable mood** qualifies; academic decline, withdrawal, somatic complaints; not normal teenage behavior

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Multifactorial mood-circuit dysfunction involving monoamines, **HPA hyperactivity with raised cortisol**, and neuroplasticity

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ MDD: **≥5 symptoms for ≥2 weeks**, including depressed mood or anhedonia; exclude mania/hypomania
Screen all adults, even asymptomatic: PHQ-2, PHQ-9 for severity; older adults: **Geriatric Depression Scale**
Interview establishes diagnosis; assess substances, drugs, TSH/CBC when clinically suspected
★ **Ask directly about suicide**, access to firearms, protective factors; questioning does not increase risk
Post-CABG anhedonia, withdrawal, fatigue → depression screen; vein-harvest leg edema expected

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Imminent danger or **severe malnutrition** → **observation, psychiatric hospitalization**; remove lethal means
Mild: CBT/interpersonal therapy; moderate/severe: sertraline + psychotherapy; pregnancy → shared risk–benefit discussion
★ Urgent suicidality/catatonia/anorexia → **ECT**; psychotic depression → ECT or antidepressant + antipsychotic
Alternatives: **bupropion** (fatigue/hypersomnia, smoking cessation), **mirtazapine** (poor appetite, insomnia)
Continue antidepressant ≥6 months after remission; recurrent/severe episodes → longer maintenance

rows.label: Complications
items: Suicide, malnutrition, functional decline, recurrence
SSRIs: sexual dysfunction, GI effects, hyponatremia; early activation/suicidality monitoring, especially age <25
Bupropion: seizures; avoid with eating disorders, seizure disorders or brain tumor; mirtazapine: weight gain/sedation
Benzodiazepines in older adults: worsen depression, sedation, falls → stop, use antidepressant

rows.label: Prevention
items: Safety plan, early follow-up after drug changes
Taper antidepressants to reduce discontinuation symptoms; avoid antidepressant monotherapy in bipolar disorder

rows.label: Mimics
items: Dementia: insidious consistent deficits; **pseudodementia**: subacute, "I don't know" answers, recall improves with prompting
Hypothyroidism: cold intolerance, constipation, elevated TSH
Untreated OSA: snoring, obesity, sleepiness → **mood disorder due to medical condition**, not MDD
Anorexia nervosa: fear of weight gain, distorted body image

table.title: Distinguishing persistent sadness
rows: Waves tied to reminders; self-esteem usually preserved
Pervasive worthlessness; bereavement does not exclude diagnosis
Stressor within 3 months; MDD criteria absent

disruptive-behavior-disorders.name: Disruptive behavior disorders
disruptive-behavior-disorders.scope: Oppositional defiant disorder (ODD), conduct disorder (CD, aggression, property destruction, rule violations, ASPD precursor), intermittent explosive disorder, parent management training, family therapy
disruptive-behavior-disorders.core: Differentiate persistent defiance, violations of others’ rights, and brief impulsive aggressive outbursts; family and behavioral interventions anchor treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Family conflict, inconsistent or harsh discipline, trauma, parental psychopathology, antisocial peers
ADHD, learning disorders, substance use can worsen behavioral dysregulation

rows.label: Clues
items: Assess aggression toward people/animals, deliberate fire-setting, theft, truancy, and running away
Callous-unemotional traits: limited remorse/empathy and shallow affect; poorer conduct-disorder prognosis
★ **Planned aggression for material gain** argues against intermittent explosive disorder

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Temperamental impulse-control vulnerability interacts with reinforcing family, peer and environmental patterns

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Multi-informant assessment**: caregivers, child, school; developmental context and functioning across settings
ODD: ≥4 symptoms; interaction with ≥1 nonsibling; frequency beyond developmental expectations
CD: ≥3 qualifying behaviors in 12 months, ≥1 in last 6 months
IED: impulsive disproportionate outbursts; age ≥6; twice weekly for 3 months or three destructive episodes/year

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Parent management training**, consistent reinforcement and consequences; family and school collaboration
Adolescent CD: multimodal/multisystemic family interventions; address safety and peer environment
★ Treat comorbid ADHD with stimulants when diagnosed; medication not routine for ODD/CD alone
Danger to others → **inpatient psychiatric admission**; refractory aggression → short-term risperidone, metabolic monitoring
IED: CBT for impulse/anger control; selected cases → fluoxetine

rows.label: Complications
items: Academic failure, family disruption, injury, legal problems, substance use
CD may precede antisocial personality disorder; adult diagnosis requires age ≥18 and CD evidence before 15

rows.label: Prevention
items: Early parenting support, trauma-informed care, learning accommodations, stable supervision and positive school supports

rows.label: Mimics
items: DMDD: persistent between-outburst irritability, onset before age 10
Bipolar disorder: distinct manic episodes with decreased need for sleep
ADHD: impulsive noncompliance without deliberate rights violations

table.title: Core distinction
rows: ≥6 months angry/argumentative/vindictive; no major rights violations
Aggression, destruction, deceit/theft, serious rule violations

hypoglycemia.name: Hypoglycemia
hypoglycemia.scope: Drug-induced hypoglycemia (insulin, sulfonylureas), Whipple triad, acute management (dextrose, glucagon), insulinoma
hypoglycemia.core: Compatible symptoms, documented low plasma glucose, and relief with correction establish Whipple triad and justify evaluation for a hypoglycemic disorder.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Insulin, sulfonylureas; missed meals, exercise, alcohol, kidney failure increase risk
Sepsis, liver failure, adrenal insufficiency; insulinoma causes fasting episodes in otherwise well adults
Child, illness, poor intake or sugar-free fluids → **glycogen depletion**, ketotic hypoglycemia ± anion-gap acidosis

rows.label: Clues
items: Adrenergic: tremor, sweating, palpitations, hunger; neuroglycopenic: confusion, visual change, seizures, coma
Autonomic neuropathy or recurrent episodes may blunt warning symptoms
★ Glucose **<54 mg/dL** clinically significant; diabetes alert threshold <70 mg/dL

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Excess insulin suppresses glucose output and ketones; substrate/hormone deficits impair counterregulation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Bedside glucose immediately**; plasma confirmation if discordant, never delay emergency correction
Critical sample: glucose, insulin, C-peptide, proinsulin, β-hydroxybutyrate, sulfonylurea screen
Suspected endogenous fasting disorder → supervised fast up to 72 h; mixed-meal test for postprandial symptoms
Biochemically confirmed insulinoma → pancreatic CT/MRI, endoscopic ultrasound if localization unclear

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Awake and swallowing → **15 g rapid carbohydrate**, recheck after 15 minutes, repeat if needed
★ Altered or unable to swallow → **IV dextrose**; no IV access → IM/intranasal glucagon
After recovery → longer-acting carbohydrate; glucagon less effective after alcohol or glycogen depletion
★ Sulfonylurea recurrence → **octreotide + dextrose**, prolonged observation; long-acting insulin may require infusion
Adjust diabetes regimen and treat trigger; localized insulinoma → surgical resection

rows.label: Complications
items: Seizures, brain injury, arrhythmias, falls; recurrent episodes cause impaired awareness
Dextrose alone after sulfonylurea exposure may stimulate further insulin release

rows.label: Prevention
items: Meal/exercise planning, glucose monitoring or CGM alarms, caregiver rescue-glucagon education
Relax overly intensive targets when recurrent events, frailty, or impaired awareness

rows.label: Mimics
items: Panic attack: normal glucose during symptoms
Stroke: focal deficit may persist after glucose correction; evaluate both if unresolved

hypoglycemia.evidence: Not checked online; established endocrine diagnostic and hypoglycemia treatment principles.

informed-consent-and-capacity.name: Informed consent and capacity
informed-consent-and-capacity.scope: Decision-making capacity, informed consent, emergency exception (implied consent), refusal of treatment, AMA discharge
informed-consent-and-capacity.core: A capable adult may accept or refuse treatment after understanding its benefits, material risks, alternatives, and consequences of refusal.

rows.label: Principle
items: ★ Capacity: **understand, appreciate (own case), reason, communicate**; decision-specific, fluctuating
Competence: legal; diagnosis, age, alcohol use, incarceration, disagreement alone ≠ incapacity

rows.label: Do
items: ★ Explain benefits, material risks, alternatives/no treatment; **qualified interpreter and teach-back**
Correct delirium, intoxication, pain, communication barriers; reassess capacity
AMA request: assess capacity, explore barriers, offer safer plan, document discussion and follow-up

rows.label: Don't
items: Capable refusal → respect choice, even if life-saving or pregnant; avoid coercion, abandonment
No valid consent → possible **battery**; signed form alone insufficient
Refusing one therapy (blood) ≠ refusing all; provide other indicated care, including surgery

rows.label: Exceptions
items: ★ Emergency + incapacity + no surrogate/directive/verified refusal → implied consent to treat
★ Parents refuse minor's life-saving transfusion → **treat emergency**; seek court authority if feasible
Incapacity without emergency → authorized surrogate; involve patient to remaining ability

rows.label: Traps
items: Psychiatric illness does not automatically remove capacity; assess the specific decision
Suicide danger may justify protective detention despite expressed desire to leave
New material procedure or changed risk → renewed consent; consent revocable anytime before procedure

table.title: Who decides
rows: Ask whom to involve; facilitate promptly; no override
Minor decides; no parental consent (state law varies)
Parents seek unproven remedy for child
Continue proven therapy; investigate remedy; CPS not first
Close; discuss after waking; no next-of-kin consent
Autonomy ≠ entitlement; physician refuses, explains, offers alternatives

informed-consent-and-capacity.evidence: Not checked online; established consent/capacity ethics; emergency and minor-consent law varies by jurisdiction.

intimate-partner-violence.name: Intimate partner violence
intimate-partner-violence.scope: Screening principles, clinical red flags, pregnancy risk, safety assessment and planning, mandatory reporting distinctions
intimate-partner-violence.core: Privately assess abuse, respect patient autonomy, and connect disclosure to immediate safety assessment and sustained support.

rows.label: Principle
items: ★ **Screen reproductive-age women**, including pregnancy/postpartum; assess concerning findings in anyone
Varied-age bruises, delayed care, controlling partner, depression, reproductive coercion → red flags
Pregnancy: abuse may begin or escalate; threatens maternal safety, worsens birth outcomes

rows.label: Do
items: ★ **Interview alone**, use professional interpreter; explain confidentiality limits before screening
Validate; document exact words/injuries; assess strangulation, weapons, threats, suicide/homicide risk
★ **Safety plan**: destination, emergency contacts, documents, advocate, ongoing support

rows.label: Don't
items: Avoid partner confrontation, blame, forced departure, or couples counseling during active abuse
Do not leave visible resources or portal messages that could endanger the patient

rows.label: Exceptions
items: ★ **Reporting laws vary**: check jurisdiction; adult IPV disclosure alone is not universally reportable
Child/elder/dependent-adult abuse, certain injuries → required reports; explain, minimize disclosure

rows.label: Traps
items: Negative screen does not exclude coercion; repeat privately when concern persists
Competent adults retain autonomy absent specific emergency/reporting duty, even when declining police
Screening alone insufficient; multicomponent continuing support provides benefit

intimate-partner-violence.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [USPSTF IPV recommendation (2025)](https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation/intimate-partner-violence-and-abuse-of-elderly-and-vulnerable-adults-screening); reporting depends on jurisdiction.

normal-pressure-hydrocephalus.name: Normal pressure hydrocephalus
normal-pressure-hydrocephalus.scope: Triad (gait apraxia/magnetic gait, cognitive impairment, urinary urgency/incontinence), ventriculomegaly on neuroimaging, high-volume lumbar puncture (Miller Fisher test), ventriculoperitoneal shunt
normal-pressure-hydrocephalus.core: An older adult develops a magnetic, short-stepped gait followed by slowed thinking and urinary urgency, with enlarged ventricles.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Often idiopathic in older adults; secondary to subarachnoid hemorrhage, meningitis, head trauma

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Gait impairment first and most prominent**: initiation difficulty, broad base, unstable turns
Frontal-subcortical dysfunction: apathy, slowed processing, executive impairment rather than early isolated amnesia
Urinary urgency can precede incontinence; complete triad unnecessary
Prominent focal deficits, severe early memory loss, or resting tremor suggest another diagnosis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Impaired CSF absorption → ventricular expansion and dysfunction of periventricular frontal-subcortical pathways
Lumbar opening pressure often normal despite disordered CSF dynamics

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Brain MRI or CT**: ventriculomegaly disproportionate to sulcal atrophy; Evans index >0.3 supportive
MRI may show tight high-convexity sulci, enlarged Sylvian fissures and periventricular signal change
★ **High-volume LP, 30–50 mL**; compare standardized gait testing before and after drainage
Improvement supports shunt responsiveness; negative tap does not exclude—consider extended lumbar drainage
Exclude obstructive hydrocephalus and assess competing neurodegenerative/vascular disease

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Selected symptomatic candidates → **ventriculoperitoneal shunt**; gait most likely to improve
Rehabilitation, fall precautions, bladder support; counsel that advanced dementia improves less reliably
No established medication reverses idiopathic NPH

rows.label: Complications
items: Untreated: falls, dependence; shunt infection, obstruction, overdrainage-related subdural hematoma
Recurrent symptoms after initial benefit → evaluate shunt malfunction

rows.label: Mimics
items: Alzheimer disease: early episodic memory loss, proportional cortical atrophy
Parkinson disease: asymmetric bradykinesia/rigidity, resting tremor, levodopa response
Hydrocephalus ex vacuo: ventricles and sulci enlarge together from tissue loss

normal-pressure-hydrocephalus.evidence: Not checked online; established NPH evaluation and shunt-selection teaching.

obsessive-compulsive-disorder.name: Obsessive-compulsive disorder
obsessive-compulsive-disorder.scope: Obsessive-compulsive disorder, ego-dystonic obsessions and compulsions, exposure and response prevention, SSRIs
obsessive-compulsive-disorder.core: Intrusive unwanted thoughts and ritualized acts consume time or impair function; treatment breaks the cycle of anxiety and neutralization.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Often begins in childhood/adolescence; family history, tic disorders, anxiety/depression comorbidity
Stress may worsen symptoms; intrusive harm/sexual thoughts do not alone imply intent

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Ego-dystonic obsessions**: contamination, doubt, symmetry, aggressive or taboo thoughts
Compulsions: washing, checking, counting or mental rituals aimed at preventing feared outcomes
Usually recognizes excessiveness, but insight ranges to absent; reassurance seeking can function as a ritual
Skin injury from washing, lateness or avoidance; severe cases markedly restrict eating or daily activity

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical dysfunction; rituals transiently reduce distress and are negatively reinforced

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical interview**: obsessions/compulsions >1 hour daily or significant distress/impairment
Assess insight, functional effect, suicidality, tics and depression; Yale-Brown scale tracks severity
Exclude substances/medical causes and distinguish repetitive behaviors driven by other disorders

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **CBT with exposure and response prevention**: graded feared-stimulus exposure without ritual completion
★ **SSRI**, e.g., sertraline/fluoxetine; mild-moderate pediatric OCD → ERP alone first; substantial impairment → combine
Often higher tolerated SSRI doses and 8–12-week trial needed; do not label failure after brief exposure
Persistent symptoms → optimize ERP/adherence, switch SSRI or clomipramine; selected resistant disease → risperidone
Reduce family accommodation/reassurance rituals; maintain effective treatment before gradual taper

rows.label: Complications
items: Depression, suicidality, social/occupational disability; dermatitis from compulsive washing
Clomipramine → anticholinergic effects, arrhythmia and overdose risk; SSRI → sexual dysfunction

rows.label: Mimics
items: Generalized anxiety: realistic everyday worries rather than intrusive obsession/neutralization cycle
Psychosis: fixed belief without typical resisted ritual; assess insight carefully

table.title: Related repetitive patterns
rows: Developmental social differences, soothing stereotyped routines
Brief involuntary movement/sound with premonitory urge

obstructive-sleep-apnea.name: Obstructive Sleep Apnea
obstructive-sleep-apnea.scope: risk factors, clinical features (excessive daytime sleepiness, snoring), polysomnography, CPAP, cardiovascular complications
obstructive-sleep-apnea.core: Recurrent upper-airway obstruction during sleep causes intermittent hypoxemia and arousals, often presenting as loud snoring and excessive daytime sleepiness.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Obesity, large neck circumference, male sex, aging, retrognathia and upper-airway crowding
Alcohol/sedatives worsen collapse; children often have adenotonsillar hypertrophy; risk rises after menopause

rows.label: Clues
items: Witnessed apneas, gasping/choking, unrefreshing sleep, morning headache, nocturia
Resistant hypertension, atrial fibrillation, secondary polycythemia or recurrent drowsy-driving episodes raise suspicion
Children may show hyperactivity, learning problems, enuresis or poor growth rather than sleepiness
Normal awake oxygen saturation does not exclude severe nocturnal disease

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Sleep-related reduction in pharyngeal tone collapses vulnerable airway despite persistent respiratory effort
Intermittent hypoxia and sympathetic surges drive hypertension; fragmentation impairs attention and vigilance
Sleep-related hypoventilation with nocturnal hypercapnia → morning headaches

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Polysomnography** confirms; screening tools such as STOP-BANG estimate risk, not diagnosis
Uncomplicated high-risk adults → home sleep apnea test acceptable; negative/inconclusive → in-laboratory study
★ AHI **≥5/hour with symptoms/comorbidity**, or ≥15 regardless of symptoms, establishes adult OSA
AHI 5–14 mild, 15–29 moderate, ≥30 severe; pediatric thresholds differ
Cardiorespiratory disease, suspected hypoventilation, chronic opioids or neuromuscular weakness → laboratory polysomnography

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **CPAP** for symptomatic OSA and most moderate/severe disease; optimize mask fit/adherence
Weight loss, exercise, lateral sleep positioning; avoid bedtime alcohol and sedatives
★ CPAP-intolerant or selected mild/moderate disease → **mandibular advancement device**
Child adenotonsillar hypertrophy → adenotonsillectomy, even with pulmonary hypertension; selected adults → surgery, hypoglossal stimulation
Counsel sleepy patients to avoid driving until controlled; do not rely on stimulants before treating obstruction

rows.label: Complications
items: Systemic hypertension, arrhythmias, stroke risk, pulmonary hypertension in selected patients
Motor vehicle/work accidents, impaired cognition, mood disturbance
Awake postoperative hypercapnia → **CPAP/BiPAP**; reintubate only if obtunded or failing noninvasive support

rows.label: Prevention
items: Maintain healthy weight, reassess after major weight change; continue PAP around surgery with monitoring

rows.label: Mimics
items: Central apnea: absent respiratory effort during pauses
Narcolepsy: cataplexy and sleep-onset REM features
OHS: persistent daytime hypercapnia

opioid-toxicity.name: Opioid toxicity
opioid-toxicity.scope: Opioid toxidrome, naloxone administration and titration, observation period, precipitated withdrawal
opioid-toxicity.core: Depressed consciousness, slow breathing, and pinpoint pupils after opioid exposure; ventilation takes priority over full awakening.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Fentanyl or heroin exposure, dose escalation, renal dysfunction, long-acting opioids
Alcohol/benzodiazepine co-ingestion; lost tolerance after detoxification, hospitalization, or incarceration

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Bradypnea or apnea** with hypoxemia; reduced bowel sounds, bradycardia, hypotension
Miosis may be absent with severe hypoxia or co-ingestion; needle marks are not required
Pulmonary edema, aspiration, hypothermia, prolonged immobilization may accompany overdose
Chronic use: daytime sleepiness, constipation, apathy, falling grades, miosis, slow breathing

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Mu-receptor activation suppresses medullary ventilatory response to CO2
Naloxone competitively reverses opioid effects but often wears off before the causative opioid

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis**; bedside glucose, pulse oximetry, capnography; do not await toxicology
Urine opiate immunoassay detects morphine/heroin/codeine; may miss fentanyl, methadone, and oxycodone
ECG for methadone-associated QT prolongation; acetaminophen level with uncertain combination-product ingestion

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Open airway, **bag-mask ventilation**, oxygen; intubate if ventilation cannot be maintained
★ **Naloxone** IV titrated to adequate breathing; intranasal/IM route if IV unavailable
Dependent but breathing: start low; apnea/no response: prompt larger/repeated doses, especially fentanyl analogs
Repeated recurrence → naloxone infusion; coma despite repeated doses → evaluate additional causes
Short-acting reversal: observe ≥4 hours after last naloxone; long-acting/recurrent sedation → prolonged monitoring/admission

rows.label: Complications
items: Anoxic brain injury, aspiration pneumonia, rhabdomyolysis, compartment syndrome
Precipitated withdrawal: agitation, vomiting, diarrhea, tachycardia; rare pulmonary edema after reversal

rows.label: Prevention
items: Take-home naloxone, overdose-response training, avoid sedative combinations; offer buprenorphine and addiction follow-up

rows.label: Mimics
items: Pontine hemorrhage: focal neurologic findings, no meaningful naloxone response
Clonidine poisoning: marked bradycardia with similar pupils
Sedative overdose: usually normal pupils; incomplete naloxone response

panic-disorder.name: Panic disorder
panic-disorder.scope: Panic attack criteria, unexpected recurrent attacks, agoraphobia, acute abortive therapy, maintenance therapy, medical rule-outs
panic-disorder.core: Recurrent unexpected panic attacks followed by at least 1 month of fear of recurrence or maladaptive behavioral change establish panic disorder.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Young adulthood, family history, trauma, anxiety sensitivity
Caffeine, stimulants, cannabis, decongestants, hyperthyroidism, withdrawal can provoke paniclike symptoms

rows.label: Clues
items: Abrupt intense fear peaks within minutes; palpitations, dyspnea, chest pain, paresthesias, derealization
Attack requires ≥4 characteristic symptoms; fear of dying/losing control common
★ **Syncope, exertional onset, hypoxemia, focal findings**, sustained arrhythmia → medical cause until evaluated
Agoraphobia: fear/avoidance of ≥2 situations where escape/help seems difficult, persisting ≥6 months

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Threat-circuit overactivation and catastrophic interpretation of benign sensations amplify autonomic symptoms
Hyperventilation lowers CO₂ → lightheadedness, perioral/distal tingling; avoidance reinforces anticipatory fear
**Sodium lactate infusion** provokes attacks: heightened panic sensitivity

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis after medical/substance review**; unexpected episodes distinguish disorder from predictable triggers
Vital signs, examination, ECG for cardiopulmonary symptoms; glucose/TSH or toxicology guided by history
Chest pain risk → ACS/PE evaluation rather than automatic psychiatric attribution
Assess depression, suicidality, substance use; agoraphobia may be diagnosed separately

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ During attack → **calm reassurance, slow breathing**, reduce stimulation after excluding danger
Severe acute episode → short-term lorazepam when needed; avoid with sedatives or substance-use risk
★ Maintenance → **CBT with interoceptive exposure and/or SSRI**, such as sertraline
Start SSRI low, titrate slowly; benefit takes weeks; venlafaxine alternative
Continue effective treatment after remission, then gradual taper; benzodiazepines not preferred long-term

rows.label: Complications
items: Agoraphobic avoidance, impaired function, depression, self-medication with alcohol
Benzodiazepine dependence/withdrawal; alprazolam → **between-dose rebound anxiety**; SSRIs may initially increase anxiety

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Reduce caffeine/stimulants**, regular sleep/exercise, practice exposure and relapse-prevention skills
Paper-bag rebreathing discouraged (hypoxemia risk); older exam questions may expect it if SpO₂ normal

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hyperthyroidism: persistent tremor, heat intolerance, low TSH
SVT: documented abrupt regular tachycardia, not solely subjective palpitations
Social anxiety: fear tied to scrutiny rather than unexpected attacks
Mitral valve prolapse: incidental click/murmur; doesn't explain recurrent attacks with fear of recurrence

panic-disorder.evidence: Not checked online; established DSM-5-TR and anxiety treatment teaching.

parasomnias.name: Parasomnias
parasomnias.scope: REM sleep behavior disorder (polysomnography, clonazepam), sleep terrors, sleepwalking (somnambulism), nightmare disorder, isolated sleep paralysis, reassurance
parasomnias.core: Unusual behavior or experiences during sleep are classified by timing, recall, and whether REM muscle atonia is lost or persists.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Sleep deprivation, stress, fever, alcohol, OSA precipitate NREM arousals
REM behavior disorder: older men, synucleinopathies, SSRIs; sleepwalking/terrors often childhood

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Dream enactment with injury** → ask bed partner about kicking, punching, falling from bed
Isolated sleep paralysis: conscious but briefly unable to move at sleep onset or awakening

rows.label: Pathophys
items: NREM disorders: incomplete arousal from deep sleep; REM behavior disorder: loss of normal skeletal atonia
Sleep paralysis: REM atonia persists into wakefulness

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Suspected REM behavior disorder → **video polysomnography** demonstrating REM without atonia
Typical childhood NREM events: clinical; atypical stereotyped episodes → video EEG/PSG
Assess snoring, sleep schedule, drugs, trauma, daytime sleep attacks

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ REM behavior disorder: **immediate-release melatonin or clonazepam**; melatonin favored with falls/OSA concerns
Sleep terrors/walking: reassurance, adequate sleep, scheduled awakenings for predictable frequent events
Nightmares: imagery rehearsal; trauma-associated nightmares → assess PTSD
Isolated paralysis: reassurance, regular sleep; accompanying cataplexy → evaluate narcolepsy

rows.label: Complications
items: Injury to sleeper/partner; clonazepam can worsen sedation, balance, sleep-disordered breathing
REM behavior disorder may precede Parkinson disease, Lewy body dementia, or multiple system atrophy

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Safe bedroom**: remove weapons, pad furniture, secure windows; separate sleeping if violent
Avoid sleep deprivation/alcohol; treat OSA; review triggering antidepressants

rows.label: Mimics
items: Nocturnal seizures: brief stereotyped clusters, possible postictal findings
OSA: gasping arousals tied to obstructive respiratory events

table.title: Timing and recall
rows: Awake, oriented, detailed frightening dream recall

personality-disorders.name: Personality disorders
personality-disorders.scope: Cluster A (paranoid, schizoid, schizotypal), Cluster B (borderline, antisocial, histrionic, narcissistic), Cluster C (avoidant, dependent, OCPD), dialectical behavior therapy
personality-disorders.core: Enduring, inflexible patterns of cognition, affect, relationships, or impulse control cause impairment across settings beginning by adolescence or early adulthood.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Temperament, genetic susceptibility, early adversity and disrupted attachment; avoid attributing diagnosis to trauma alone
Traits must exceed cultural expectations; diagnose cautiously during acute illness or developmental transitions

rows.label: Clues
items: Cluster A: paranoid—distrust; schizoid—detachment; schizotypal—magical thinking, odd speech/perceptions, social discomfort
Cluster B: antisocial—violations of rights; histrionic—attention seeking; narcissistic—grandiosity/entitlement
Cluster C: avoidant—fears rejection/embarrassment, avoids new activities; dependent—clinging; OCPD—rigid perfectionism, control
★ Borderline: **splitting, unstable identity/relationships, self-harm**, abandonment fear, chronic emptiness, impulsivity

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Maladaptive trait patterns impair emotion regulation and interpersonal functioning; no diagnostic biomarker
Impulsive aggression, violent suicide → **low CSF 5-HIAA** (serotonin metabolite)

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Longitudinal clinical assessment** across contexts; obtain collateral with consent
Exclude mood episodes, psychotic illness, substances, neurodevelopmental disorders and acquired brain disease
★ Antisocial diagnosis requires **age ≥18 plus conduct disorder before 15**
Borderline may cause brief stress-related paranoia/dissociation; sustained psychosis requires broader evaluation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Borderline → **dialectical behavior therapy**; structured psychotherapy and consistent team boundaries
Trait-matched psychotherapy, e.g., avoidant → **CBT**, assertiveness training; clear expectations, empathic, nonpunitive tone
No medication treats personality disorder globally; target comorbid depression/anxiety or limited severe symptoms
Self-harm threats → assess intent, plan, access and safety; imminent risk → emergency psychiatric care
Avoid staff splitting through shared care plans; avoid reflexive long-term benzodiazepines in impulsive patients

rows.label: Complications
items: Self-injury/suicide, substance misuse, impaired work/relationships; antisocial traits → legal or violence consequences
Stigma and inconsistent treatment worsen engagement; therapeutic ruptures require careful repair

rows.label: Mimics
items: Autism: early developmental social-communication differences and restricted interests
Delusional disorder: fixed delusion rather than generalized suspicious personality style

personality-disorders.evidence: Not checked online; established clinical teaching.

table.title: Common diagnostic confusions
rows: Reactive hours-long shifts vs sustained mood episodes
Odd beliefs vs persistent frank psychosis

phobias.name: Phobias
phobias.scope: Specific phobia (flying, heights, blood-injection-injury), exposure therapy, situational benzodiazepines, social anxiety disorder (generalized vs performance-only), beta-blockers, agoraphobia
phobias.core: Persistent disproportionate fear leads to avoidance or endurance with intense distress, producing impairment despite recognition that danger is limited.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Temperamental inhibition, family anxiety, frightening experiences or learned fear; often childhood/adolescent onset

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Fear reliably provoked by trigger; duration **≥6 months**, excessive relative to actual/cultural danger
Anticipatory anxiety and avoidance limit school, work, medical care or travel
Blood-injection-injury subtype may produce vasovagal syncope rather than persistent tachycardia

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Conditioned threat response and avoidance prevent extinction; relief from escape reinforces fear

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical assessment** of trigger, feared consequence, avoidance and impairment
Agoraphobia: fear in ≥2 categories—transport, open/enclosed spaces, crowds/lines, outside home alone
Exclude substances, hyperthyroidism, arrhythmia or pulmonary disease when bodily symptoms atypical
Symptoms only with feared trigger, normal exam → psychiatric evaluation, not pheochromocytoma/Holter workup

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Graded exposure-based CBT** first-line across phobic disorders
Blood-injection-injury: applied muscle tension during exposure reduces fainting
Generalized social anxiety: CBT or sertraline/escitalopram; venlafaxine alternative
★ Performance-only social anxiety → situational **propranolol**; asthma/bradycardia → short-acting benzodiazepine instead
Rare trigger (flight, MRI) → short-acting benzodiazepine (**↑GABA-A**); routine use risks dependence, impairs exposure

rows.label: Complications
items: Social/occupational restriction, depression, substance misuse; avoidance of necessary health care
Beta-blocker hypotension; benzodiazepine sedation, falls, impaired driving

rows.label: Prevention
items: Early treatment, repeated graduated practice and reduced avoidance help maintain gains
Avoid self-medication with alcohol; include relapse-prevention exposure plans

rows.label: Mimics
items: Panic disorder: recurrent unexpected attacks; fear of further attacks
OCD: intrusive obsessions and rituals drive avoidance
Avoidant personality: pervasive longstanding inadequacy/rejection sensitivity, often coexists with social anxiety

phobias.evidence: Social anxiety care checked 2026-10-30: [NIMH](https://www.nimh.nih.gov/health/publications/social-anxiety-disorder-more-than-just-shyness); established exposure-based care.

physiologic-changes-of-aging.name: Physiologic changes of aging
physiologic-changes-of-aging.scope: Neurologic changes, sensory changes (presbyopia, presbycusis), sleep architecture changes (early wake, reduced total sleep), cardiovascular stiffening, renal decline, pulmonary compliance
physiologic-changes-of-aging.core: Normal aging reduces organ reserve; preserved everyday independence distinguishes expected slowing from disease.

rows.label: Definition
items: Gradual changes across systems; marked disability requires evaluation rather than attribution to age
Presbyopia: reduced accommodation; presbycusis: bilateral high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss

rows.label: Interpret
items: ★ Slower processing and recall; **orientation and learned knowledge preserved**
★ Less slow-wave, more awakenings, earlier timing, less total sleep → **reassure**, no hypnotics
★ Isolated **↓ankle reflexes**, ↓toe vibration, impaired tandem, full strength → normal; no workup

rows.label: Use when
items: Reduced baroreflexes and maximal heart rate → orthostatic susceptibility, reduced exercise capacity
Lower renal clearance → adjust renally eliminated drugs despite normal-looking creatinine
Decreased vital capacity and cough reserve → greater respiratory illness vulnerability

rows.label: Compare
items: ★ **Arterial stiffness** → widened pulse pressure; ventricular relaxation slows
Reduced lung elastic recoil → increased lung compliance; chest wall compliance decreases
Declining concentration/dilution → fluid imbalance; reduced muscle mass lowers creatinine production

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Delirium, dementia, falls, incontinence** require evaluation; never inevitable normal aging
Depression or sedatives can explain daytime sleepiness; severe insomnia needs investigation
Unilateral hearing loss, focal weakness, **rotatory nystagmus**, rapid memory loss → disease workup

physiologic-changes-of-aging.evidence: Not checked online; established geriatric physiology.

polyuria-diabetes-insipidus.name: Polyuria and diabetes insipidus
polyuria-diabetes-insipidus.scope: Central diabetes insipidus, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (lithium, hypercalcemia), water deprivation test, desmopressin response
polyuria-diabetes-insipidus.core: Large-volume dilute urine requires separation of water diuresis from solute diuresis; impaired thirst or water access makes diabetes insipidus dangerous.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Central: sellar surgery/trauma/infiltration; nephrogenic: lithium, hypercalcemia, hypokalemia or inherited defects
Primary polydipsia: excessive voluntary intake, psychiatric disease; osmotic diuresis: diabetes mellitus, mannitol

rows.label: Clues
items: Polyuria >3 L/day in adults, nocturia, polydipsia; distinguish from frequent small-volume voiding
★ **Hypernatremia with urine osmolality <300 mOsm/kg** suggests inadequate antidiuretic effect
Low/low-normal sodium favors excess drinking; dehydration, weakness or altered mentation signals severe water deficit

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Insufficient vasopressin signaling prevents collecting-duct aquaporin-mediated water reabsorption
Lithium enters collecting-duct cells through ENaC and impairs concentrating ability

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Confirm **24-hour urine volume**; serum Na/osmolality, urine osmolality, glucose, calcium, K, creatinine
Hyperglycemia with concentrated solute-rich urine → osmotic diuresis; no need for water deprivation
★ Stable hypotonic polyuria → **supervised water deprivation followed by desmopressin**, or stimulated copeptin testing
Avoid dehydration testing in existing hypernatremia/volume depletion; partial defects may yield overlapping responses
Established central disease → pituitary MRI and anterior-axis evaluation; check lithium level with exposure

rows.label: Tx
items: Shock → isotonic resuscitation first; then oral/IV free water with serial sodium monitoring
★ Central → **desmopressin**; avoid excess water intake and monitor for hyponatremia
Nephrogenic → remove cause, low-solute diet, thiazide; lithium-associated → amiloride
Lithium toxicity → stop drug, isotonic fluids; severe neurologic effects/impaired clearance → hemodialysis consultation
Primary polydipsia → address cause and supervised intake plan; desmopressin risks water intoxication

rows.label: Complications
items: Hypernatremic encephalopathy, seizures, hypovolemic shock; overly rapid chronic sodium correction → cerebral edema
Desmopressin/excess drinking → hyponatremic seizures; chronic lithium → CKD

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Reliable water access, sick-day plan; lithium renal/electrolyte monitoring and avoidance of volume depletion
Mild lithium DI, intact thirst, normal sodium → **keep drinking**; fluid restriction risks hypernatremic dehydration

rows.label: Mimics
items: Overactive bladder/UTI: frequency without increased total volume
Postobstructive diuresis: follows relief of retention; monitor fluid/electrolyte losses

polyuria-diabetes-insipidus.evidence: Testing update checked 2026-10-30: [Endotext AVP deficiency/resistance, 2026](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK279011/); classic testing patterns: established teaching.

post-traumatic-stress-disorder.name: Post-traumatic stress disorder
post-traumatic-stress-disorder.scope: PTSD diagnostic criteria (>1 month: intrusion, avoidance, negative mood/cognition, hyperarousal), acute stress disorder (<1 month), trauma-focused psychotherapy (CBT, EMDR), SSRIs, prazosin for nightmares
post-traumatic-stress-disorder.core: Persistent trauma-linked reexperiencing and avoidance with altered mood and heightened arousal cause functional impairment beyond the immediate stress response.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Exposure to actual/threatened death, serious injury or sexual violence; direct, witnessed, or qualifying indirect exposure
Prior trauma, psychiatric illness, repeated exposure, poor social support

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Intrusion**: nightmares, flashbacks, distress with reminders; avoidance of internal/external cues
Negative beliefs, guilt, detachment or trauma amnesia; hypervigilance, exaggerated startle, sleep disturbance
Dissociative subtype: depersonalization or derealization; severe distress may coexist with suicidality

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Persistent dysregulated threat response and impaired contextual extinction of traumatic fear

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Clinical: ≥1 intrusion, ≥1 avoidance, ≥2 negative mood/cognition, ≥2 arousal symptoms
**>1 month**, impairment, and not better explained by substances or another illness
Assess ongoing danger, self-harm risk, substance use, depression and traumatic brain injury

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ First-line **trauma-focused psychotherapy**: prolonged exposure, cognitive processing therapy, or EMDR
★ If medication preferred/needed → **sertraline, paroxetine, or venlafaxine**; premature ejaculation → paroxetine (delays ejaculation)
Prazosin for persistent trauma nightmares; monitor orthostatic hypotension, not an overall PTSD treatment
Avoid benzodiazepines; no established benefit and increased dependence risk
Immediate safety planning and psychiatric hospitalization when imminent self-harm or inability to remain safe

rows.label: Complications
items: Depression, substance use disorders, suicide risk, relationship and occupational impairment

rows.label: Prevention
items: Early practical support, **psychoeducation normalizing trauma reactions**; symptomatic acute stress → trauma-focused CBT
Avoid compulsory single-session psychological debriefing; maintain supportive follow-up

rows.label: Mimics
items: Adjustment disorder: stress-related distress without required trauma or full PTSD syndrome
Panic disorder: unexpected attacks without obligatory trauma-linked symptoms

table.title: Time course
rows: Full criteria first met ≥6 months later

schizophrenia-spectrum-disorders.name: Schizophrenia spectrum disorders
schizophrenia-spectrum-disorders.scope: Brief psychotic disorder, schizophreniform disorder, schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder, mesolimbic dopamine
schizophrenia-spectrum-disorders.core: Psychosis with impaired reality testing: distinguish schizophrenia-spectrum disorders by duration, functional decline, and the relationship between mood episodes and psychosis.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Family history, neurodevelopmental vulnerability; adolescent cannabis exposure increases risk
Typical onset late adolescence/early adulthood; exclude stimulant, hallucinogen, medication, and neurologic causes

rows.label: Clues
items: Delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech/behavior; negative symptoms: avolition, alogia, flat affect
★ At least **two core symptoms**, including delusions, hallucinations, or disorganized speech, for active-phase diagnosis
Suicidality, dangerous commands or inability to eat → urgent safety assessment

rows.label: Pathophys
items: ★ **↑Mesolimbic dopamine** → positive symptoms; mesocortical → negative symptoms, early working-memory deficits
D2 blockade reduces psychosis but nigrostriatal/tuberoinfundibular effects cause EPS and hyperprolactinemia
Structural correlate: **enlarged lateral and third ventricles**, reduced cortical volume

rows.label: Dx
items: Clinical history, collateral information, mental status; assess mood timeline and substance exposure
First episode → CBC/CMP, TSH, toxicology; HIV/syphilis or neuroimaging for relevant risks/atypical neurologic findings
★ **Schizoaffective**: ≥2 weeks psychosis without mood episode; mood episodes occupy most illness duration

rows.label: Tx
items: Safety crisis → hospitalization; acute agitation → de-escalation, then medication if needed
★ **Risperidone, aripiprazole or olanzapine** + coordinated specialty care, family education, CBT, supported employment
Schizoaffective depressive/bipolar subtype → add antidepressant or mood stabilizer according to mood syndrome
★ Failure of two adequate antipsychotic trials or persistent substantial suicide risk → **clozapine**
Adherence difficulty → long-acting injectable (haloperidol decanoate); catatonia → lorazepam, then ECT if refractory

rows.label: Complications
items: Suicide, homelessness, substance use, cardiometabolic disease; antipsychotics → metabolic syndrome, tardive dyskinesia, NMS
Clozapine → neutropenia, myocarditis, severe constipation; monitor ANC and symptoms

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid cannabis/stimulants; maintenance medication, relapse planning reduce recurrence
Monitor weight, BP, glucose, lipids; address tobacco use and cardiovascular risk
**High expressed emotion** (family criticism, hostility) → relapse; family therapy reduces recurrence

rows.label: Mimics
items: Mood disorder with psychosis: psychosis occurs exclusively during mood episodes
Delirium: fluctuating attention/awareness and acute medical cause
Delusional disorder: ≥1 month delusions with otherwise relatively preserved function, limited other psychotic symptoms
Substance/medication-induced psychosis: recent stimulants (mydriasis, tremor) or corticosteroids, intact orientation

sexual-dysfunction.name: Sexual dysfunction
sexual-dysfunction.scope: Female orgasmic disorder, female sexual interest/arousal disorder, genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder, premature ejaculation, SSRI-induced sexual dysfunction
sexual-dysfunction.core: Persistent, distressing impairment of desire, arousal, orgasm, ejaculation, or penetration; classify the affected phase before choosing treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Depression, anxiety, relationship conflict, sexual trauma, menopause
Diabetes, neurologic disease, pelvic surgery; SSRIs, antipsychotics, opioids

rows.label: Clues
items: Interest/arousal: ↓interest, fantasies, initiation, pleasure, cue response, genital sensations; assess adequate stimulation
★ Penetration pain/fear, pelvic-floor spasm blocking tampon/speculum → genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder (**vaginismus**)
Low lubrication, vaginal dryness, postcoital spotting → assess estrogen deficiency

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Serotonergic inhibition of sexual response; hypoestrogenism → mucosal atrophy
Performance anxiety and pain avoidance reinforce dysfunction
Bilateral oophorectomy → ↓**ovarian androgens** → low libido despite estrogen replacement, normal vaginal mucosa

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Symptoms usually ≥6 months + personal distress; frequency criteria depend on disorder
Private sexual/relationship history; review drugs, coercion, mood, and medical causes
Pelvic examination for pain; TSH, prolactin, glucose only when history suggests abnormality
Low desire without distress → normal variation; inadequate stimulation alone ≠ orgasmic disorder

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Education, couples/sex counseling, CBT; treat underlying disease and relationship contributors
Penetration disorder → pelvic-floor physical treatment, graded dilators; vaginal estrogen for menopausal atrophy
★ SSRI-induced: reduce dose if feasible, switch to or augment with **bupropion**
Acquired generalized HSDD: flibanserin in women <65, including postmenopause; separate from alcohol
Flibanserin: avoid hepatic impairment and moderate/strong CYP3A4 inhibitors; not for drug-induced low desire

rows.label: Complications
items: Avoidance, relationship strain, reduced quality of life
Flibanserin: syncope; topical penile anesthetics: partner numbness

rows.label: Mimics
items: Vulvodynia: localized provoked vestibular tenderness
Major depression: pervasive anhedonia beyond sexual situations
Normal aging: slower response without clinically significant distress

sexual-dysfunction.evidence: FDA label checked 2026-10-30: [flibanserin, 2025](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2025/022526s013lbl.pdf); other content established teaching.

somatic-symptom-disorders.name: Somatic symptom disorders
somatic-symptom-disorders.scope: Somatic symptom disorder, illness anxiety disorder, conversion disorder, factitious disorder, malingering, regular scheduled visits, validating suffering
somatic-symptom-disorders.core: Distressing symptoms or health fears require a positive psychiatric formulation, validation, and proportionate medical evaluation; intent separates factitious behavior from functional symptoms.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Trauma, anxiety/depression, chronic illness, major stress; medical and psychiatric disorders can coexist

rows.label: Clues
items: Persistent reassurance seeking, repeated testing, high health-related distress, impaired function
Assess suicidality, abuse, substance use, and medication-related symptoms; avoid assumptions based on demographics
Functional blindness: intact **pupillary reflex, threat blink, optokinetic nystagmus**
Extreme fever + normal pulse/labs → suspect falsification; **supervised rectal temperature** before antibiotics

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Attention, threat appraisal, and learned responses amplify suffering; symptoms do not require conscious production
External reward differs from internal sick-role motivation; neither can be inferred from one inconsistency

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Somatic symptom disorder does not require medically unexplained symptoms**; excessive response is decisive
Illness anxiety requires ≥6 months preoccupation; somatic symptom persistence typically >6 months
★ Functional neurologic: **incompatible signs**: Hoover, give-way weakness, midline sensory split, forehead vibration discrepancy
Nonepileptic seizures: captured spell without **video-EEG** epileptiform change; often acute stressor
New objective abnormalities still warrant targeted medical evaluation; avoid diagnosing solely by exhaustive exclusion

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **One clinician, scheduled visits**, focused examinations; validate suffering without endorsing unproven disease
CBT, functional rehabilitation, treat comorbid anxiety/depression
Functional deficits → empathic explanation, expected recovery; nonepileptic seizures → **CBT**, no antiseizure drugs
★ Functional deficit or negative workups → **psychiatric assessment**, no more procedures; **new red flags → reassess**
Factitious: team approach, factual records, no confrontation, evaluate psychiatric comorbidity; protect dependents from induced illness

rows.label: Complications
items: Iatrogenic injury, unnecessary surgery, opioid exposure, disability, fragmented care
Factitious disorder imposed on another → serious abuse risk requiring safeguarding action

rows.label: Mimics
items: Occult medical disease: evolving objective findings or coherent physiologic abnormalities
Delusional disorder: fixed somatic belief despite evidence, without flexible doubt

table.title: Distinguishing patterns
rows: Motor/sensory symptoms incompatible with neurologic disease
Intentional deception; no obvious external reward
Intentional symptoms, external gain; no treatment/invasive testing

somatic-symptom-disorders.evidence: Not checked online; established DSM-5-TR teaching.

substance-use-disorders.name: Substance use disorders
substance-use-disorders.scope: Diagnostic criteria (mild, moderate, severe), cocaine use disorder, amphetamine use disorder, cannabis use disorder, motivational interviewing, cognitive behavioral therapy, 12-step programs
substance-use-disorders.core: A problematic pattern causing impaired control, risky use, social impairment or physiologic adaptation defines substance use disorder; severity follows criterion count.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Family history, trauma, psychiatric comorbidity, early exposure, unstable housing and peer availability
Persistent psychosocial stress and limited treatment access worsen trajectory

rows.label: Clues
items: Tolerance/withdrawal not required; physiologic adaptation during prescribed use alone does not establish disorder
Stimulant withdrawal: fatigue, hypersomnia, depression and craving; assess suicide risk
Cannabis withdrawal: irritability, anxiety, insomnia and reduced appetite after sustained use
Caffeine withdrawal: diffuse headache 12–48 h after stopping intake, including NPO surgery; normal neurologic exam

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Reward learning and neuroadaptation strengthen cue-driven behavior while impairing control
Cocaine blocks monoamine reuptake; amphetamines increase release; cannabinoids act mainly at CB1 receptors
THC lipophilic, adipose-stored: urine positive for weeks in chronic use; other drugs clear in days

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **≥2 of 11 DSM-5 criteria in 12 months**; severity **mild 2–3, moderate 4–5, severe ≥6**
Control/social: larger/longer use, failed cutdown, time spent, craving, role failure, social problems, abandoned activities
Risk/pharmacologic: hazardous use, continued despite physical/psychological harm, tolerance, withdrawal
Clinical interview establishes disorder; urine drug testing documents exposure, not severity or current impairment
Screen co-occurring depression, psychosis, HIV/hepatitis risk and polysubstance use; confirm unexpected immunoassay positives

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Motivational interviewing**: explore ambivalence, elicit personal goals, support autonomy; avoid confrontation
★ Stimulant disorder → **contingency management**, CBT/community reinforcement; no FDA-approved maintenance drug
Cannabis disorder → motivational enhancement, CBT and contingency management; no established approved medication
Peer/12-step programs as adjuncts; tailor outpatient versus residential intensity to safety/support and impairment
Stimulant agitation → benzodiazepines/cooling; uncomplicated cannabis intoxication, mild paranoia → observe, no drugs

rows.label: Complications
items: Cocaine/amphetamine → MI, stroke, arrhythmia, psychosis; chronic methamphetamine → cardiomyopathy and dental injury
Cannabis → impaired driving, hyperemesis (cessation, fluids, capsaicin/haloperidol), anxiety or psychosis
Stimulant crash can precipitate severe depression/suicidality; withdrawal usually lacks alcohol-like autonomic danger
Older adults: new benzodiazepine (temazepam) → subacute ataxia, dysarthria, confusion, falls

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Harm reduction: **naloxone** for possible opioid contamination, avoid using alone, offer fentanyl testing access
Treat comorbid illness, relapse planning, overdose education and regular follow-up; recurrence prompts reassessment
Adolescent experimentation without impairment → counsel teen and family; no formal treatment program

rows.label: Mimics
items: Bipolar mania: episodes persist independently of intoxication
Primary psychosis: symptoms outside substance exposure periods
ADHD: longstanding childhood-onset pattern, not episodic intoxication

substance-use-disorders.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ASAM/AAAP stimulant guideline 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11105801/); DSM-5 criteria established definitions.

Violent agitation, hyperthermia; formication with excoriations; MDMA empathic
Red conjunctivae, dry mouth, tachycardia, hunger, slowed time

Perioral/perinasal rash, solvent odor, ataxia/slurring; clears <1 hour
Coma, apnea, hypotension, bradycardia, sluggish pupils

suicide-risk-assessment.name: Suicide risk assessment
suicide-risk-assessment.scope: Risk and protective factors, lethal means restriction, hospitalization criteria, safety planning
suicide-risk-assessment.core: Assess current suicidal intent, plan, access, past behavior, and ability to remain safe; imminent danger requires immediate protection.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior attempt strongest historical predictor; depression, bipolar disorder, psychosis, substance use, chronic pain
Recent loss, isolation, incarceration/discharge, agitation, hopelessness, firearm access; older men have high fatality risk

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Plan + intent + available lethal means**, preparations, or recent attempt → high acute risk
Command hallucinations, intoxication, severe insomnia, impulsivity, inability to collaborate increase concern
Giving away possessions or sudden calm after despair can signal resolved intent

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Acute distress, impaired judgment, and accessible lethal methods can convert transient suicidal urges into fatal acts
Protective connections and restricted means increase time and opportunity for intervention

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Ask directly** about ideation, intent, plan, timing, access, prior attempts; asking does not induce suicide
Depression or hopelessness, even with somatic complaints → assess suicide risk **before further medical workup**
Assess depression/mania, psychosis, substance use, violence risk, medical contributors, collateral information
Use structured instruments to support assessment, never as a sole disposition rule
Intoxicated patient → observation and reassessment when clinically sober; initial denial is insufficient

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Imminent danger → **constant observation, remove hazards, emergency psychiatric evaluation/hospitalization**
Voluntary admission preferred; involuntary protection if serious danger and refusal, following local law
Treat poisoning/injury first; address agitation, withdrawal, mood/psychotic disorder and underlying medical illness
Low acute risk with reliable support → outpatient care only with collaborative plan and rapid follow-up

rows.label: Complications
items: Fatal or repeated attempts, hypoxic injury, disability, caregiver distress
High vulnerability after emergency/inpatient discharge; abrupt loss of contact raises concern

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Safety plan**: warning signs, coping actions, supportive contacts, professional crisis resources, emergency escalation
★ **Lethal means restriction**: secure/remove firearms, limit medication quantities; enlist trusted support
Arrange prompt follow-up and active care linkage; identify reasons for living and dependable supervision

rows.label: Mimics
items: Nonsuicidal self-injury: no intent to die, but future suicide risk still elevated
Passive death wish: no active plan, still warrants full evaluation
Obsessive intrusive harm thoughts: unwanted/ego-dystonic, without desire or intent to act

suicide-risk-assessment.evidence: Not checked online; established clinical suicide-risk assessment and safety-planning principles; detention law varies locally.

sympathomimetic-toxicity.name: Sympathomimetic toxicity
sympathomimetic-toxicity.scope: Cocaine, amphetamines, methamphetamine, sympathomimetic toxidrome, benzodiazepines, cooling, avoidance of pure beta-blockers
sympathomimetic-toxicity.core: Stimulant exposure produces agitation, diaphoresis, mydriasis, hypertension, tachycardia, and hyperthermia; sedation limits dangerous catecholamine excess.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Cocaine, amphetamines, methamphetamine, synthetic cathinones; prescription stimulant misuse
Coingested alcohol forms cocaethylene with cocaine, increasing cardiotoxicity; exertion/heat worsens injury

rows.label: Clues
items: Paranoia, psychosis, seizures, chest pain; bowel sounds usually active
★ **Severe hyperthermia, acidosis, rigidity/agitation, arrhythmia** → life-threatening poisoning
Cocaine additionally blocks sodium channels, producing QRS widening
MDMA: bruxism, diaphoresis, hyperthermia, severe **hyponatremia** from water intake and SIADH

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Cocaine inhibits monoamine reuptake; amphetamines increase release → adrenergic/dopaminergic overstimulation
Vasoconstriction, increased oxygen demand, platelet activation → myocardial/cerebral ischemia

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical toxidrome**; temperature, glucose, ECG, electrolytes, creatinine, CK, urinalysis
Chest pain → serial ECG/troponin; neurologic deficit/severe headache → head CT for hemorrhage/stroke
Urine immunoassay supports exposure but false positives/negatives occur; never delay stabilization for results

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Benzodiazepines first** for agitation, seizures, tachycardia, hypertension; airway support when necessary
★ **Rapid external cooling + IV crystalloids** for hyperthermia/rhabdomyolysis; antipyretics ineffective
Persistent severe hypertension/vasospasm → nitroglycerin, nicardipine, or phentolamine after sedation
★ Acute cocaine toxicity: **avoid pure beta-blocker monotherapy**; unopposed alpha vasoconstriction concern
Wide QRS ventricular toxicity → sodium bicarbonate; ACS evaluation and aspirin when bleeding contraindications absent

rows.label: Complications
items: MI, aortic dissection, ischemic/hemorrhagic stroke, seizures, rhabdomyolysis, AKI, DIC
Methamphetamine: formication, dental decay, psychosis, cardiomyopathy; cocaine snorting: rhinitis, septal perforation; pregnancy: abruption

rows.label: Prevention
items: Offer addiction treatment and contingency management; assess depression and suicidality after stimulant crash
Harm-reduction counseling, avoid mixing substances; naloxone access for possible opioid contamination

rows.label: Mimics
items: Anticholinergic toxicity: dry skin, urinary retention, reduced bowel sounds
Serotonin syndrome: inducible/spontaneous clonus, hyperreflexia; NMS: dopamine blockade, lead-pipe rigidity
Thyroid storm: thyroid disease with sustained systemic hypermetabolism
PCP: rotatory/vertical nystagmus, violent agitation; also sedate with benzodiazepines

wernicke-korsakoff-syndrome.name: Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome
wernicke-korsakoff-syndrome.scope: Wernicke encephalopathy (triad of encephalopathy, ataxia, oculomotor dysfunction), Korsakoff psychosis (confabulation, amnesia), thiamine (B1) deficiency, IV thiamine before glucose, mammillary body atrophy
wernicke-korsakoff-syndrome.core: Malnourished adult with confusion, gait ataxia, or ophthalmoplegia/nystagmus; the complete Wernicke triad is often absent.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Alcohol use disorder, hyperemesis gravidarum, bariatric surgery, starvation, inadequate parenteral nutrition
IV dextrose, carbohydrate loading or refeeding increases thiamine demand → precipitates Wernicke in depleted patients

rows.label: Clues
items: Ocular: nystagmus, **bilateral lateral rectus (CN VI) palsy**, conjugate-gaze palsy; wide-based gait
Hypothermia, hypotension, or coma signal severe deficiency
★ Korsakoff: disproportionate **anterograde amnesia**, retrograde memory loss, confabulation; relatively preserved alertness

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Thiamine deficiency impairs carbohydrate metabolism → ATP failure and selective neuronal injury
Medial thalami, periaqueductal gray, mammillary bodies injured → persistent amnestic syndrome

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis**; do not wait for vitamin assays or imaging before treatment
MRI may show symmetric thalamic/periaqueductal lesions; normal MRI does not exclude Wernicke
Chronic disease: mammillary body atrophy; evaluate glucose, electrolytes, magnesium, and competing encephalopathy causes

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected Wernicke → **high-dose IV thiamine**, followed by oral replacement after stabilization
**IV thiamine before or with dextrose**, hypoglycemia included; if thiamine unavailable, never delay dextrose
Replete magnesium, fluid/electrolyte deficits; restore nutrition cautiously and treat alcohol withdrawal separately
Ocular findings may improve rapidly; gait/cognition recover more slowly; established amnesia often persists

rows.label: Complications
items: Untreated encephalopathy → death or irreversible Korsakoff syndrome; falls and impaired independent living
Refeeding syndrome → hypophosphatemia, arrhythmias, respiratory weakness

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Routine oral **thiamine supplementation** for persistent malnutrition; nutritional assessment during alcohol treatment
Alcohol cessation support, balanced nutrition; monitor intake after bariatric surgery or prolonged vomiting

rows.label: Mimics
items: Alcohol withdrawal delirium: autonomic hyperactivity, tremor, hallucinations after reduced intake
Hepatic encephalopathy: cirrhosis, asterixis, precipitating bleed or infection
Posterior circulation stroke: abrupt focal deficits; diffusion MRI identifies infarction

wernicke-korsakoff-syndrome.evidence: Not checked online; established thiamine-deficiency teaching.
